reason: The text contains clear evidence of structured collaboration between leaders and people, particularly in the latter portion describing Jehoshaphat's judicial reforms. Jehoshaphat appoints judges throughout the fortified cities of Judah (וַיַּעֲמֵ֨ד שֹֽׁפְטִ֜ים בָּאָ֗רֶץ בְּכָל־ עָרֵ֧י יְהוּדָ֛ה). He then establishes an explicit working relationship where judges, priests (including the chief priest Amariah), officials (Zebadiah), and Levite officers collaborate with the people to hear disputes and administer justice (וְכָל־ רִיב אֲשֶׁר־ יָב֨וֹא עֲלֵיכֶ֜ם מֵאֲחֵיכֶ֣ם הַיֹּשְׁבִ֣ים בְּעָרֵיהֶ֗ם). Additionally, the earlier narrative shows various groups—kings, prophets, and armies—working together toward common objectives (וְלָעָם אֲשֶׁר עִמּ֑וֹ). The instruction emphasizing unity (בֶּאֱמוּנָה וּבְלֵבָב שָׁלֵם—'in faithfulness and with a whole heart') reinforces this collaborative theme.
